html:
Basava was a 12th-century minister, poet and reformer in Karnataka who founded the Lingayat tradition. His dates are uncertain; many accounts put his death about 1167.

He was born a Brahmin and is said to have thrown off his sacred thread as a boy. He rose to be treasurer to King Bijjala at Kalyana. There he gathered a circle of devotees of Shiva from every caste and trade: a cobbler, a washerman, a boatman, and women such as the poet Akka Mahadevi. They met in a hall called the Anubhava Mantapa, the hall of experience.

His teaching was plain:

  • there is one god, Shiva, and each person wears his sign, a small linga, on the body;
  • temples, priests and rituals are not needed;
  • caste and the idea of pollution are false, and men and women are equal;
  • work is worship.

He taught through vachanas, short prose poems in everyday Kannada. They are the start of Kannada literature for ordinary readers and part of the wider bhakti movement.

About 1167 his followers held a wedding between a Brahmin girl and an untouchable boy. The king had the fathers put to death, the city rose, Bijjala was killed and the group scattered. Lingayats are now one of the largest communities in Karnataka.
